title: Yigdal
hook: Maimonides' thirteen principles put into verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adon Olam, the poem that ends with sleep. Your line was I shall not fear. Today, its partner, a song that holds a whole philosophy.

Start with a dense page of philosophy: careful, argued, written in Arabic by a doctor and rabbi, Moses Maimonides, inside his commentary on the Mishnah. It lists thirteen things he says a Jew must hold to be true. Now jump to a congregation on a Friday night, swaying, singing those same thirteen ideas to a bright melody. Somewhere between the two, the list became a short Hebrew song, sung in many synagogues at the end of Friday night services. Philosophy, set to music.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S DENSE PAGE.` → `THIRTEEN PRINCIPLES.` → `SET TO MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Yigdal means may he be magnified. It opens: magnified be the living God, and praised. The poem is usually credited to Daniel ben Judah, who lived in Rome in the fourteenth century. He did something clever: he took Maimonides' thirteen principles and gave each one a line. God exists. God is one. God has no body. God is first and last. Only God is to be worshipped. The prophets spoke truly. Moses was the greatest of the prophets. The Torah was given from heaven. It won't be exchanged. God knows our deeds. God rewards and punishes. The redeemer will come. And the dead will live again, the hope the song ends on. Now the honest part. Maimonides' list was never the only way to say what Judaism believes. Other thinkers argued with it. Joseph Albo, in Spain, boiled the roots of faith down to three. Others asked whether faith can be a checklist at all, when so much of Judaism is about what you do. Still, the list lasted, in songs like this one, and in a prose version, each line beginning I believe with perfect faith, printed in many prayer books after the morning service. Yigdal turns a debate into something a child can sing. In this tradition, ideas travel not only in books, but in the mouth.
screen: `MAY HE BE MAGNIFIED.` · `THIRTEEN PRINCIPLES, THIRTEEN LINES.` · `OTHERS ARGUED: ALBO SAID THREE.` · `A DEBATE A CHILD CAN SING.` · then, large: `FAITH IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Don't reach for the biggest belief you have; find one that's true for you today, about God, or people, or how you want to live, or an honest doubt, and put it into one short sentence. Say it out loud once, quietly, and hear how it sounds in the air instead of in your head.
Yigdal. May he be magnified. Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith, set as a thirteen-line song.
Your line: faith in verse. Thirteen beliefs, and a tune to carry them. Day six hundred six, done.

howItsDone: Yigdal is printed at the start of the morning service in many prayer books and is often sung at the end of Friday night and festival evening services; a prose version of the thirteen principles, each beginning 'I believe with perfect faith', appears in many siddurim.

chat.says: Is Yigdal just a happy closing song, or does it actually say something?
options: It sets Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith to music, one per line.
It lists the Ten Commandments in rhyme so children can learn them.
It retells the Exodus from Egypt, verse by verse, for the Sabbath.

Yigdal.meaning: may he be magnified; a song of thirteen principles

Maimonides.meaning: a medieval rabbi, doctor and philosopher

Mishnah.meaning: the early rabbis' collection of Jewish law and teaching

Daniel ben Judah.meaning: a poet of Rome usually credited with Yigdal

Joseph Albo.meaning: a thinker in Spain who named three roots of faith

sources.ref: Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10:1 (introduction to Perek Chelek)

notes: Authorship: usually credited to Daniel ben Judah of Rome (14th century); confirm.
The list of thirteen principles is condensed in plain words; confirm order and wording.
Albo's three roots (God's existence, revelation, reward and punishment); confirm.
Maimonides wrote the commentary in Judeo-Arabic; 'in Arabic' simplified.
Some communities (e.g., some Hasidic rites) do not say Yigdal; not mentioned.
